subject: mathematics
question_text: By the Gauss-Jordan method, solve 2x + 4y − z = 0, x + 2y + 2z = 5, 3x + 6y − 7z = 2.

mark_split.label: Clear column 1 below the leading entry
Reach the impossible row and read it
State that there is no solution

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.34 — LAQ chapter 3 Matrices, answer 20.4. This answer carries NO printed year tag, so `appearances` is empty; it is in the book on merit rather than on frequency. It is the second of only two questions in the whole Matrices chapter whose answer is not a single triple — the other is answer 20.3, which has infinitely many. The two are a deliberate pair and are best studied together: both end with a row whose coefficients are all zero, and the ONLY thing that separates them is whether the constant after the rule is zero too. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S. Book p.34 sets two questions side by side in two columns, leaving no margin for the [N Marks] tags the chapter uses elsewhere. The 1+2+1+2+1 above is deliberately the same shape used for the other three Gauss-Jordan answers in this unit. The row-operation chain is the book's own. Star rank is the CHAPTER's ★★★, not this question's. Paper position: Maths-1A Section C runs Q18-Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this by the Gauss-Jordan method — and say what it means if a row ends up with all zeros on the left but not on the right.

steps.label: Write the augmented matrix
steps.margin_note: First mark. Look at the x and y coefficients: 2 and 4, then 1 and 2, then 3 and 6 — every row has y twice x. Columns 1 and 2 are proportional, which is the first hint that this system will not behave.
lines: The system in matrix form is AX = D, where

lines.text: A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 6 & -7 \end{bmatrix}, \ X = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix}, \ D = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 5 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}

recall.must_convey: That the augmented matrix [A | D] is written — the coefficient matrix with the constants column attached.
accept: write the augmented matrix A D with the constants joined to the coefficient matrix
form A given D by putting the right hand side as a fourth column
write the coefficient matrix together with the constants column
augmented matrix rasta, coefficients tho patu constants column kuda
attach the constants to A to make the augmented matrix

steps.why: The method is identical whatever the answer turns out to be. You cannot tell from the question that this system has no solution — the working is what tells you.
common_mistakes: Spotting the proportional columns and writing 'no solution' straight away; that is a guess, not a proof.
Writing A alone and losing the constants.

steps.label: Clear column 1
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Row 2 already starts with a 1, so swap it to the top first. Then clear column 1 as usual — and watch column 2 go to zero along with it.

recall.must_convey: That rows are swapped to get a leading 1, then row 1 is used to clear column 1 — and that column 2 clears at the same time.
accept: swap rows to get a one on top then subtract multiples of row one to clear the first column and the second clears too
exchange row one and row two then eliminate below the leading one
use the leading one to make both the first and second columns zero below it
row one row two swap chesi, R2 minus 2R1 and R3 minus 3R1 cheyyali
get a one at the top left then knock out the entries under it

steps.why: Columns 1 and 2 are proportional, so clearing one clears the other. That leaves only z with a live coefficient — two equations about one unknown, which is one equation too many.
common_mistakes: Clearing column 1 before getting a leading 1 and introducing fractions.
Assuming the zero second column is an arithmetic error.

steps.label: Make the lower pivots 1
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Divide each of the bottom two rows by its own leading number. Now both rows claim to fix z — and they claim different values, which is the contradiction about to surface.
lines: Row 2 says z = 2 and row 3 says z = 1.

recall.must_convey: That the bottom two rows are divided by their leading entries to become 0 0 1, and that they then disagree about the value of z.
accept: divide row two by minus five and row three by minus thirteen so both become zero zero one but with different constants
normalise the bottom rows and they give z equals two and z equals one which disagree
make both lower pivots one and the two rows contradict each other about z
rendu rows ni divide cheste zero zero one avthai kani z values veru veru
the two bottom rows both fix z but at different values

steps.why: z cannot be 2 and 1 at the same time. The next step turns that plain observation into the standard form an examiner is looking for.
common_mistakes: Dividing the coefficients but not the constant after the rule.
Picking one of the two z values and carrying on with it.

steps.label: Reach the impossible row
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Subtracting the identical rows leaves zeros on the left of the rule but −1 on the right. Read that row back as an equation and it says 0 = −1, which nothing can satisfy.
lines: Row 3 read back as an equation is

recall.must_convey: That the last row becomes 0 0 0 with a NON-zero constant, and that reading it back gives 0 = −1, which is impossible.
accept: row three becomes all zeros on the left but minus one on the right which says zero equals minus one and that is impossible
subtract the two identical rows and the last row reads zero equals minus one
the final row gives zero x plus zero y plus zero z equals minus one which cannot happen
last row zero zero zero kani constant minus one, ante zero equals minus one, adi impossible
the coefficients vanish but the constant does not so the equation is a contradiction

steps.why: This is the ONE thing that separates this question from the infinite-solution one. There the zero row had a zero constant and said 0 = 0, which is harmlessly true. Here the constant survives, and the row says something false.
common_mistakes: Writing 'infinite solutions' because a row went to zeros, without checking the constant.
Crossing the zero row out as though it were empty.
Reporting z = 2 from row 2 as if part of the answer had been salvaged.

steps.label: State that there is no solution
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Say it plainly and say why. 'No solution' with the impossible equation quoted beside it is the complete answer — there is nothing else to write.
lines: Since one equation of the equivalent system
cannot be satisfied by any x, y, z:

recall.must_convey: That the system has NO solution, and that the reason is the impossible row — not merely that the working stopped.
accept: the system has no solution because one equation says zero equals minus one
there is no solution since a row gives an impossible equation
no values of x y and z can satisfy the system so there is no solution
system ki solution ledu, endukante oka equation impossible
the equations are inconsistent so no solution exists

steps.why: Geometrically the three equations are three planes with no common point. Saying 'no solution' answers the question; quoting the row that proves it is what earns the mark.
common_mistakes: Writing 'no solution' with no reason given.
Leaving the answer blank because no numbers were found; 'no solution' IS the answer here.
Confusing this with the infinite-solution case.
